                     DATA CENTERS AND LARGE
                             LOADS

      A Community Protection, Siting and Lifecycle Framework

                              Executive Brief

                              September 2026

                   Jonathan P. Saunders, MFA, LL.M.
                           Saunders Consigliere, PLLC
                 180 State Street, Suite 225, Southlake, TX 76092
               Saunders@saundersconsigliere.com | 682-417-2968

Ask better questions. Obtain better information. Make informed decisions.
                                                                   DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF



Purpose of This Framework
This framework does not advocate for or against data-center development. Data centers can bring
investment, tax revenue, infrastructure and other benefits, while also creating significant demands for
electricity, water, land and public infrastructure.
Its purpose is narrower and more practical: to identify the questions public officials and communities
should ask before making decisions whose consequences may last for decades.
Many of the most important questions are not obvious from a development application, public
presentation or economic-impact statement. They concern ultimate ownership, financial responsibility,
infrastructure costs, electricity supply, water availability, future expansion, operational impacts,
changes in ownership, financial security, modernization, closure and decommissioning.
The objective is not to determine the decision. It is to improve the information on which the decision is
made.
An informed community may approve a project, reject it, modify it or impose conditions upon it. That
choice belongs to the community and its elected officials. This framework is intended to help them
understand what they should know before making it.
  Ask better questions. Obtain better information. Make informed decisions.

Executive Brief
America is entering a period of data-center development on a scale for which many existing regulatory
systems were not designed.
Artificial intelligence, cloud computing and other digital services are driving proposals for facilities
requiring hundreds of megawatts and, in some cases, campuses whose projected electrical demand
approaches or exceeds that of substantial cities. These projects may require new generation,
transmission facilities, substations, water supplies, wastewater capacity, roads and emergency services.
Their effects can extend well beyond the property on which they are constructed. Communities are
increasingly questioning electricity costs, water consumption, noise, backup generation, tax incentives,
infrastructure requirements and the cumulative effects of multiple projects. Some jurisdictions have
imposed or considered moratoriums while determining whether existing rules are adequate.
Congress has also entered the debate. The House passed H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, on
September 16, 2026, by a vote of 417-3. The Senate is considering S. 5199, the GRID Savings Act of 2026,
introduced by Senator Martin Heinrich of New Mexico.
Both bills address an important but narrower question: who should bear the electrical-system costs
created by exceptionally large new loads?
Electricity, however, is only one part of the inquiry. Water consumption may be equally significant,
particularly where communities face limited supplies, population growth, drought, competing
demands or infrastructure constraints. A sound review therefore should determine what resources a
particular project will require, in what quantities, from what sources, for how long, under what
operating conditions, and at whose cost and risk.
  What protections should government establish before approving a major data- center
  development, and how should those protections remain enforceable throughout the
  project's life?

A large data-center campus should not be evaluated merely as a building seeking land-use approval or
as an electrical customer seeking interconnection. It is a long-duration infrastructure commitment



                                                    1
                                                                      DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


involving the developer, utility, ratepayers, water suppliers, local government and surrounding
community.

Approval therefore should consider the project's entire lifecycle:
Applicant -> financing -> siting -> construction -> interconnection -> operation -> modernization ->
expansion -> ownership or operator change -> financial distress -> closure -> decommissioning -> site
restoration.

The Time Horizon Matters
The expected life of the proposed facility should be established early.
A data center may involve infrastructure investments and public commitments designed to last for
decades while the computing equipment inside the facility has a substantially shorter technological life.
Buildings, electrical infrastructure, water systems and other improvements may remain through
multiple generations of servers, cooling systems, business models and owners.
Government therefore should distinguish among several different time horizons:

  Equipment life != facility life != infrastructure life != economic life !=
  regulatory approval life.
The question is not merely how long today's equipment will operate. It is the expected lifecycle of the
site and its supporting infrastructure, including foreseeable modernization, expansion, ownership
changes, eventual closure and decommissioning.
Long-term financial assurance, infrastructure-cost allocation, water commitments, tax incentives and
decommissioning requirements should be evaluated against those differing time horizons rather than
an assumption that the project will continue operating indefinitely.
A particularly important question follows:
  What happens if the public or utility infrastructure outlives the private investment for
  which it was constructed?

1. The Regulatory Gap
Current regulation is fragmented.
Federal and state energy law, utility regulators, grid operators and utilities divide responsibility for
electricity generation, transmission, interconnection, reliability and rates. Water governance may
involve state agencies, groundwater districts, river authorities, municipal utilities, regional authorities
and other suppliers. Local governments exercise varying authority over land use, development,
infrastructure, roads, noise, emergency services and other community effects.
Those divisions can obscure whether anyone is evaluating the project's combined demands on the
community.
A determination that adequate electrical service can be provided does not establish that adequate
water is available. The existence of a water source does not establish that generation, transmission and
distribution capacity can be provided without significant cost or reliability consequences.
No single approval necessarily answers the fundamental questions:
Who ultimately owns and financially supports the project?
Who pays for infrastructure constructed principally or substantially to serve it, and who owns,
operates, maintains and ultimately replaces that infrastructure?



                                                     2
                                                                    DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


What happens if projected demand never materializes, the project is only partially built, or the facility
closes prematurely?
What quantities of electricity and water will the project require under normal and constrained
conditions?
What happens when ownership, control, technology or operating methods change?
Who pays for decommissioning and restoration if the responsible project entity lacks sufficient assets
when those obligations arise?
These are not secondary details. They determine whether promises made during approval remain
meaningful ten, twenty or thirty years later.

2. From Policy Objective to Enforceable Obligation
The emerging federal proposals illustrate a larger regulatory problem.
H.R. 9340 and S. 5199 demonstrate recognition of the potential consequences of extraordinarily large
electrical loads and the importance of determining who bears associated system costs.
They also illustrate a recurring drafting problem: a policy objective is not the same thing as an
enforceable obligation.
Terms governing incremental costs, necessary facilities, causation, cost responsibility, financial
assurance, interconnection and comparable regulatory treatment can allocate enormous financial
obligations. Ambiguity does not disappear after enactment or approval. It moves downstream - to
regulators, utilities, grid operators, administrative proceedings and ultimately courts.
Every material protection should therefore answer several basic questions:
Who is obligated? Identify the specific legal entity responsible for performance. “The developer,” “the
project” or “the data center” may be inadequate when multiple affiliates, utilities, contractors,
operators or special-purpose entities are involved.
What precisely must that party do? Required performance should be definite enough to determine
compliance. Terms such as reasonable efforts, appropriate measures, minimize, mitigate, or fair share
may require objective standards or additional definition.
When must it be done? An obligation without a deadline, triggering event, frequency, duration or
completion standard may be difficult to enforce.
How is performance measured and verified? Where practicable, requirements should establish
measurable criteria - megawatts, gallons, decibels, emissions, traffic volumes, completion dates,
financial amounts, operating hours or other appropriate metrics - and identify reporting, testing,
inspection or independent verification requirements.
Who bears the cost? The governing instrument should identify who pays for construction, operation,
monitoring, maintenance, repair, replacement and other associated costs.
What financial security supports the obligation? Where performance may be required years or
decades later, government should determine whether a parent guarantee, bond, letter of credit,
reserve, insurance or other financial assurance is necessary and how its adequacy will be maintained.
What happens when circumstances change? The framework should address foreseeable changes in
technology, demand, water availability, electricity requirements, ownership, project scale and
operating methods.
What happens upon transfer of ownership or control? Material obligations should not inadvertently
disappear when the project, property, operating company or controlling ownership changes.

                                                    3
                                                                   DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


What is the consequence of nonperformance? An obligation without an effective enforcement
mechanism may amount to little more than an aspiration.
  Do not regulate by intention. Regulate by defined obligation, measurable standard,
  identified responsibility, documented verification, financial security and enforceable
  consequence.

Broad language can create the appearance of protection without establishing an enforceable standard.
A representation that a project will “minimize water consumption” does not by itself establish a water
standard. An enforceable provision identifies permitted consumption, measurement methodology,
reporting requirements, drought provisions, exceptions, verification and consequences.
A commitment to “mitigate noise” is incomplete unless applicable limits, measurement locations,
methodology, operating conditions, monitoring requirements and consequences are established.
Likewise, a promise that a developer will pay its “fair share” of infrastructure costs raises immediate
questions: What share? Determined by whom? Using what methodology? Payable when? Adjusted how
if circumstances change?
The time to resolve those questions is before approval and substantial investment - not after the parties
have acquired conflicting economic and legal interests in what the language means.

3. Know the Counterparty
Every major data-center review should determine who is actually behind the application.
A special-purpose entity with a project name and limited assets may be the legal applicant without
being the economic entity controlling the development.
Government should identify, as applicable:
• the property owner;
• the project developer;
• the ultimate parent and controlling ownership;
• the intended data-center operator;
• principal equity participants and project lenders;
• the utility counterparty;
• entities responsible for construction;
• entities responsible for environmental and operational compliance;
• the entity responsible for closure, decommissioning and restoration;
• the owner of material project infrastructure; and
• any guarantor or other entity providing financial assurance.
The jurisdiction should then map responsibility obligation by obligation.
Property ownership, development, financing, operation, utility service, infrastructure ownership,
environmental compliance and decommissioning may reside in different entities, some of which may
be special-purpose companies with limited assets.
For each material obligation, government should know which entity is legally responsible, whether
that entity has the financial capacity to perform, whether another entity guarantees its performance,
and whether the obligation survives transfer, restructuring, foreclosure, bankruptcy, change of
operator or change of control.

                                                       4
                                                                  DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


A commitment should not be accepted merely because someone associated with the project made it.
The entity making the commitment should possess the legal authority, operational control and financial
capacity necessary to perform it.
Where material obligations depend upon the financial strength of an affiliated company, an
appropriate guarantee or other financial assurance may be necessary.
Material changes in ownership or control should not automatically extinguish protections negotiated
with the original developer.

4. The Cost Principle
The starting economic principle should be straightforward:
  Existing residents and businesses should not involuntarily subsidize infrastructure whose
  need is materially created by a new large-load project without an explicit public
  determination authorizing that allocation.

Applying that principle requires more than saying “the developer pays.” The governing framework
should address generation, transmission, substations, distribution facilities, water and wastewater
infrastructure, roads, emergency-response capacity and other project-driven public expenditures.
It should also determine what happens when assumptions change.
What if infrastructure is constructed for a projected 500-MW load but the project ultimately uses 200
MW?
What if a planned campus is only partially constructed or the customer terminates service before
infrastructure costs are recovered?
What if an improvement serves both the data center and existing customers?
What if the project is sold, expanded or substantially modernized?
What if project-funded infrastructure later serves other customers?
What if infrastructure remains useful after the data center reduces operations or closes?
These circumstances require predetermined allocation, adjustment and reconciliation rules addressing
both initial costs and material changes over the project's life.
  Otherwise, “the developer pays” is a slogan rather than a cost-allocation system.

5. Approval Is the Beginning, Not the End
Traditional development regulation frequently concentrates on whether a project may be built. For
infrastructure of this magnitude, that is insufficient.
The governmental framework should continue through operation and eventual closure. It should
address periodic reporting, compliance verification, inspection rights where authorized, expansion,
financial-assurance reviews, ownership and operator changes, material changes in electricity or water
demand, enforcement and decommissioning.
Continuing oversight also requires someone to be responsible for it.
Before approval, the jurisdiction should identify the official, department, agency or other body
responsible for receiving reports, monitoring deadlines, reviewing compliance information, following
up on deficiencies and initiating enforcement when necessary.
A requirement that is never monitored may provide little practical protection regardless of how
carefully it was drafted.


                                                   5
                                                                   DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


A project approved at 300 MW should not necessarily become a 900-MW project merely because
sufficient land remains within the development. A facility approved using one cooling technology
should not necessarily adopt a substantially more water-intensive system without review. A change in
operator should not cause negotiated commitments to disappear.
Nor should closure leave taxpayers responsible for obsolete infrastructure or restoration of an
abandoned industrial site.

Modernization and Retrofit
Modernization can extend the useful life of existing facilities and infrastructure and may reduce
energy, water or other impacts. It can also materially change the project originally reviewed and
approved.
New computing and cooling technologies may increase electrical demand, alter water requirements,
require additional generation or transmission, change noise or emissions characteristics, or increase
the operating intensity of the site.
The original approval therefore should distinguish routine equipment replacement from material
modifications requiring additional review.
The relevant question is not whether the owner calls a change an “upgrade,” “retrofit” or
“modernization.” It is whether the change materially alters the assumptions, resource demands or
community impacts upon which the original approval was based.
  Approval creates a continuing regulatory relationship, not a one-time permission slip.

6. Timing, Construction Capacity and Delivery Risk
A project may be financially committed, publicly announced and even under construction before all of
the generation, transmission, water, utility and other infrastructure necessary for full operation is
physically available. Approval therefore should distinguish between infrastructure that is planned,
financed, permitted or contracted and infrastructure that will actually be operational when each
increment of load is energized.
The relevant schedule is not simply the data center's construction schedule. It is the integrated schedule
for the data center, generation, transmission, substations, fuel supply, water and wastewater facilities,
roads, communications and other dependencies required for operation.
A credible sequencing analysis should identify each material dependency, the entity responsible for
delivering it, the date on which it must be available, the consequences of delay and the party that bears
the resulting cost and risk.
Construction capacity is itself one of those dependencies. Large data-center campuses can require
sustained concentrations of electricians, mechanical and HVAC trades, controls specialists, concrete
crews, civil and utility contractors, commissioning personnel and other skilled workers. The same
regional labor pool may also be needed to build the generation, transmission and utility infrastructure
required to serve the project.
Much of that risk is contractually transferred to prime contractors and subcontractors through fixed-
price, schedule, manpower, completion, indemnity and bonding requirements. That allocation does not
create workers who are unavailable. A critical subcontractor that cannot maintain its workforce,
defaults, or withdraws can disrupt multiple dependent trades. Performance bonds and other security
may protect against financial loss, but replacement of a major specialty contractor can itself consume
time, increase cost and threaten the project schedule.



                                                    6
                                                                     DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


The effect may extend beyond the project. A multiyear data-center build can offer skilled workers
sustained employment, overtime, per diem and compensation that smaller contractors, homebuilders,
public works contractors and ordinary commercial projects cannot match. The resulting competition
can increase regional construction costs and delay unrelated housing, infrastructure and commercial
development.

Illustrative Texas Experience
Texas already provides a practical warning. Reporting from Abilene describes residential builders and
electrical contractors losing experienced electricians to major data-center construction, with resulting
housing delays. Separate 2026 construction-market analysis identifies Texas as one of the concentrated
data-center markets in which skilled-trade constraints are increasing costs and making labor
availability a material project-delivery issue.
The lesson is broader than any single project or trade. A jurisdiction evaluating a major large-load
development should ask not only whether the developer has a construction plan, but whether the
regional contractor and skilled-labor market can support the data center and its supporting
infrastructure on the schedules being represented without creating unexamined cost, completion or
community consequences.
Planned capacity is not delivered capacity. Contractual responsibility is not physical capability. Both
should be tested before schedules and public commitments are accepted.

7. Financial Structure, Debt and Continuity Risk
A project's financial capacity should not be treated as a fact established once at approval. It can change
materially during construction, commissioning and operation. Large data-center developments may be
financed through combinations of parent-company capital, project-level debt, leases, special-purpose
entities, customer commitments, guarantees and other contractual arrangements. The legal entity
holding the permit or property may therefore be only one part of the financial structure supporting
performance.
The central public question is not whether the project uses debt. It is whether the financial structure
remains capable of supporting the obligations on which approval depends.
That inquiry becomes particularly important when a developer, operator, tenant, guarantor or
affiliated enterprise is simultaneously supporting multiple facilities in different stages of development.
A company may have one campus operating, another commissioning, several under construction and
additional projects requiring capital. Financial stress at one level of that structure can affect decisions
about completion, expansion, maintenance, infrastructure payments or continued operation
elsewhere.
Government therefore should understand the principal sources of project capital; material project debt
and lease obligations; the identity and scope of guarantors; whether guarantees are limited by amount,
duration or project; and whether public obligations depend upon continued performance by a tenant,
customer, parent or affiliate that is not itself the permit holder.
The framework should also address foreseeable stress scenarios. What happens if construction costs
materially exceed budget? If commissioning is delayed? If anticipated revenue or customer demand
does not materialize on schedule? If refinancing becomes unavailable or materially more expensive? If
a major tenant, operator or guarantor defaults? If capital must be allocated among several affiliated
projects at the same time?
Those questions matter because public and utility infrastructure may already have been constructed
when financial stress emerges. A financially troubled project should not be able to transfer


                                                     7
                                                                                                   DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


unrecovered infrastructure costs, deferred maintenance, environmental obligations, decommissioning
costs or other project-specific liabilities to ratepayers or taxpayers merely because the original
financial assumptions failed.
Financial assurance should therefore be tested not only for its existence at approval, but for its
durability. Guarantees, bonds, letters of credit, reserves and other protections should be evaluated for
amount, duration, renewal, draw conditions, priority, replacement requirements and survival through
restructuring, foreclosure, bankruptcy, ownership change or operator change.
  Financial capacity is not static. Approval should test both the project's ability to perform
  under expected conditions and the protections that remain if those conditions deteriorate.

8. The Minimum Community Protection Framework
Before approval of a major data-center or comparable large-load development, the responsible
governmental bodies should be able to answer at least these questions:
1. Identity and control: Who owns, controls, finances and operates the project?
2. Financial responsibility: What entity possesses sufficient resources to satisfy the project's long-term
obligations?
3. Electricity: What are the expected and maximum anticipated loads, how will electricity be supplied,
what new infrastructure is required, and who pays for it?
4. Stranded-cost protection: What happens if the projected load is delayed, reduced or abandoned?
5. Generation adequacy: What additional generation or firm capacity is required to serve the load
without impairing reliability?
6. Timing and sequencing: For each increment of new load, what generation, transmission, fuel, water
and other supporting infrastructure will be physically operational - not merely planned, permitted,
financed or announced - when that load is energized, and what happens if a required dependency is
late?
7. Water: What are expected and maximum withdrawals, what source will supply them, what
infrastructure is required, and what happens during drought or other supply constraints?
8. Noise: What enforceable limits apply at property lines and affected residences, including low-
frequency and nighttime noise, and how will compliance be measured?
9. Backup generation: How much generating capacity will be installed, what fuel will it use, under what
circumstances may it operate, and how will emissions and noise be controlled?
10. Transportation and construction: Who bears road, traffic and infrastructure impacts during
construction and operation?
11. Construction workforce and subcontractor capacity: Is sufficient qualified labor and specialty-
contractor capacity demonstrably available for site work, utilities, vertical construction, electrical,
mechanical, controls and commissioning, and what contingency exists if a critical contractor cannot
perform or must be replaced?
12. Regional construction-market effects: How may the project's multiyear labor demand affect wages,
contractor availability, housing, public works, commercial construction and the simultaneous
construction of generation, transmission and other infrastructure required to serve the project?
13. Emergency services: What additional fire, hazardous-material, security and emergency- response
capacity is required, and who pays?
14. Expansion: What changes in load, buildings, generating capacity, cooling systems or operations
require renewed governmental review?
15. Transfer: What happens when ownership, control or the operator changes?

                                                                           8
                                                                                                   DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


16. Monitoring: What information must be reported, how frequently, who reviews it, and how can
government independently verify it?
17. Enforcement: What happens when a material requirement is violated?
18. Financial security: What guarantees, bonds, letters of credit, reserves or other security protect long-
term obligations, and how will their adequacy be maintained?
19. Closure: Who pays for decommissioning, removal and restoration, and is that obligation financially
secured before it becomes necessary?
20. Infrastructure ownership and maintenance: Who will own, operate, maintain, repair and ultimately
replace infrastructure constructed principally or substantially to serve the project?
21. Infrastructure after closure: What happens to project-related infrastructure if the facility closes, and
can it economically and safely serve another development or public purpose?
22. Modernization and retrofit: Which equipment replacements or technological upgrades may occur
under the existing approval, and what material changes in electricity, water, cooling, generation,
emissions, noise or other impacts require renewed review?
23. Project lifecycle: What are the expected economic and physical lives of the equipment, facility and
supporting infrastructure, and what assumptions underlie those estimates?
24. Governmental oversight: Which public body or official is responsible for receiving reports, verifying
continuing compliance, tracking financial assurances and initiating enforcement throughout the
project's life?
25. Cumulative effects: What other large-load developments are existing, approved or reasonably
anticipated in the area, and what are their combined effects on electricity, water, infrastructure, public
services, construction capacity and regional labor markets?
26. Financial resilience and continuity: How is construction and operation financed; what material
debt, lease, guarantee or customer obligations support the project; and what protections remain if the
owner, developer, operator, tenant, guarantor or affiliated enterprise experiences cash-flow stress,
default, refinancing difficulty or competing capital demands across multiple projects?

Conclusion
The United States needs computing infrastructure. Communities also have legitimate interests in
reliable electricity, affordable utility service, adequate water, functioning infrastructure, reasonable
environmental conditions and protection against long-term liabilities created by private development.
Those objectives are not inherently incompatible. Nor does this framework presume that a proposed
data center should be approved or rejected.
The emerging federal debate over ratepayer protection addresses an important part of the problem,
but electricity costs are only one component of a larger set of questions involving water, infrastructure,
ownership, financial responsibility, operations, modernization, community impacts and eventual
closure.
  Large-load development requires lifecycle governance.

Before approval, government should know who is responsible, what that party must do, who pays, who
owns and maintains supporting infrastructure, whether required infrastructure and construction
capacity will actually be available when needed, how compliance will be measured and independently
verified, what financial security stands behind material obligations, whether the financial structure can
withstand foreseeable stress, and what happens when circumstances change.




             Saunders Consigliere, PLLC | 180 State Street, Suite 225, Southlake, TX 76092 | Saunders@saundersconsigliere.com | 682-417-2968
                                                                           9
                                                                                                  DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOADS | EXECUTIVE BRIEF


The same discipline should continue after approval. Material commitments should be monitored,
financial assurances maintained, significant changes reviewed, and responsibilities preserved through
changes in ownership, operation, technology and project configuration.
This framework is intended not to determine a community's decision, but to ensure that the decision is
made with a clear understanding of the project's obligations, costs, risks and long- term consequences.
  Those questions should be answered before commitments become irreversible - not years
  later in a courtroom.

2. From Policy Owective to Enforceable Obligation
The emerging federal proposals illustrate a larger regulatory problem.
H.R. 9340 and S. 5199 demonstrate recognition of the potential consequences of extraordinarily large
electrical loads and the importance of determining who bears associated system costs.
They also illustrate a recurring drafting problem: a policy objective is not the same thing as an
enforceable obligation.
Terms governing incremental costs, necessary facilities, causation, cost responsibility, financial
assurance, interconnection and comparable regulatory treatment can allocate enormous financial
obligations. Ambiguity does not disappear after enactment or approval. It moves downstream - to
regulators, utilities, grid operators, administrative proceedings and ultimately courts.
Every material protection should therefore answer several basic questions:
Who is obligated ? Identify the specific legal entity responsible for performance . " The developer , „„ the
project" or "the data center" may be inadequate when multiple affiliates, utilities, contractors,
operators or special-purpose entities are involved.
What precisely must that party do? Required performance should be definite enough to determine
compliance. Terms such as reasonable efforts, appropriate measures, minimize, mitigate, or fair share
may require objective standards or additional definition.
When must it be done? An obligation without a deadline, triggering event, frequency, duration or
completion standard may be difficult to enforce.
How is performance measured and verified? Where practicable, requirements should establish
measurable criteria - megawatts, gallons, decibels, emissions, traffic volumes, completion dates,
financial amounts, operating hours or other appropriate metrics - and identify reporting, testing,
inspection or independent verification requirements.
Who bears the cost? The governing instrument should identify who pays for construction, operation,
monitoring, maintenance, repair, replacement and other associated costs.
What financial security supports the obligation? Where performance may be required years or
decades later, government should determine whether a parent guarantee, bond, letter of credit,
reserve, insurance or other financial assurance is necessary and how its adequacy will be maintained.
What happens when circumstances change? The framework should address foreseeable changes in
technology, demand, water availability, electricity requirements, ownership, project scale and
operating methods.
What happens upon transfer of ownership or control? Material obligations should not inadvertently
disappear when the project, property, operating company or controlling ownership changes.

What is the consequence of nonperformance? An obligation without an effective enforcement
mechanism may amount to little more than an aspiration.
  Do not regulate by intention. Regulate by defined obligation, measurable standard,
  identified responsibility, documented verification, financial security and enforceable
  consequence.
Broad language can create the appearance of protection without establishing an enforceable standard.
A representation that a project will "minimize water consumption" does not by itself establish a water
standard. An enforceable provision identifies permitted consumption, measurement methodology,
reporting requirements, drought provisions, exceptions, verification and consequences.
A commitment to "mitigate noise" is incomplete unless applicable limits, measurement locations,
methodology, operating conditions, monitoring requirements and consequences are established.
Likewise, a promise that a developer will pay its "fair share" of infrastructure costs raises immediate
questions: What share? Determined by whom? Using what methodology? Payable when? Adjusted how
if circumstances change?
The time to resolve those questions is before approval and substantial investment - not after the parties
have acquired conflicting economic and legal interests in what the language means.

3. Know the Counterparty
Every major data-center review should determine who is actually behind the application.
A special-purpose entity with a project name and limited assets may be the legal applicant without
being the economic entity controlling the development.
Government should identify, as applicable:
• the property owner;
• the project developer;
• the ultimate parent and controlling ownership;
• the intended data-center operator;
• principal equity participants and project lenders;
• the utility counterparty;
• entities responsible for construction;
• entities responsible for environmental and operational compliance;
• the entity responsible for closure, decommissioning and restoration;
• the owner of material project infrastructure; and
• any guarantor or other entity providing financial assurance.
The jurisdiction should then map responsibility obligation by obligation.
Property ownership, development, financing, operation, utility service, infrastructure ownership,
environmental compliance and decommissioning may reside in different entities, some of which may
be special-purpose companies with limited assets.
For each material obligation, government should know which entity is legally responsible, whether
that entity has the financial capacity to perform, whether another entity guarantees its performance,
and whether the obligation survives transfer, restructuring, foreclosure, bankruptcy, change of
operator or change of control.

A commitment should not be accepted merely because someone associated with the project made it.
The entity making the commitment should possess the legal authority, operational control and financial
capacity necessary to perform it.
Where material obligations depend upon the financial strength of an affiliated company, an
appropriate guarantee or other financial assurance may be necessary.
Material changes in ownership or control should not automatically extinguish protections negotiated
with the original developer.

4. The Cost Principle
The starting economic principle should be straightforward:
  Existing residents and businesses should not involuntarily subsidize infrastructure whose
  need is materially created by a new large-load project without an explicit public
  determination authorizing that allocation.
Applying that principle requires more than saying "the developer pays." The governing framework
should address generation, transmission, substations, distribution facilities, water and wastewater
infrastructure, roads, emergency-response capacity and other project-driven public expenditures.
It should also determine what happens when assumptions change.
What if infrastructure is constructed for a projected 500-MW load but the project ultimately uses 200
MW?
What if a planned campus is only partially constructed or the customer terminates service before
infrastructure costs are recovered?
What if an improvement serves both the data center and existing customers?
What if the project is sold, expanded or substantially modernized?
What if project-funded infrastructure later serves other customers?
What if infrastructure remains useful after the data center reduces operations or closes?
These circumstances require predetermined allocation, adjustment and reconciliation rules addressing
both initial costs and material changes over the project's life.
  Otherwise, "the developer pays" is a slogan rather than a cost-allocation system.

5. Approval Is the Beginning, Not the End
Traditional development regulation frequently concentrates on whether a project may be built. For
infrastructure of this magnitude, that is insufficient.
The governmental framework should continue through operation and eventual closure. It should
address periodic reporting, compliance verification, inspection rights where authorized, expansion,
financial-assurance reviews, ownership and operator changes, material changes in electricity or water
demand, enforcement and decommissioning.
Continuing oversight also requires someone to be responsible for it.
Before approval, the jurisdiction should identify the official, department, agency or other body
responsible for receiving reports, monitoring deadlines, reviewing compliance information, following
up on deficiencies and initiating enforcement when necessary.
A requirement that is never monitored may provide little practical protection regardless of how
carefully it was drafted.

A project approved at 300 MW should not necessarily become a 900-MW project merely because
sufficient land remains within the development. A facility approved using one cooling technology
should not necessarily adopt a substantially more water-intensive system without review. A change in
operator should not cause negotiated commitments to disappear.
Nor should closure leave taxpayers responsible for obsolete infrastructure or restoration of an
abandoned industrial site.
Modernization and Retrofit
Modernization can extend the useful life of existing facilities and infrastructure and may reduce
energy, water or other impacts. It can also materially change the project originally reviewed and
approved.
New computing and cooling technologies may increase electrical demand, alter water requirements,
require additional generation or transmission, change noise or emissions characteristics, or increase
the operating intensity of the site.
The original approval therefore should distinguish routine equipment replacement from material
modifications requiring additional review.
The relevant question is not whether the owner calls a change an " upgrade , „„ retrofit " or
"modernization." It is whether the change materially alters the assumptions, resource demands or
community impacts upon which the original approval was based.
  Approval creates a continuing regulatory relationship, not a one-time permission slip.

6. Timing, Construction Capacity and Delivery Risk
A project may be financially committed, publicly announced and even under construction before all of
the generation, transmission, water, utility and other infrastructure necessary for full operation is
physically available. Approval therefore should distinguish between infrastructure that is planned,
financed, permitted or contracted and infrastructure that will actually be operational when each
increment of load is energized.
The relevant schedule is not simply the data center's construction schedule. It is the integrated schedule
for the data center, generation, transmission, substations, fuel supply, water and wastewater facilities,
roads, communications and other dependencies required for operation.
A credible sequencing analysis should identify each material dependency, the entity responsible for
delivering it, the date on which it must be available, the consequences of delay and the party that bears
the resulting cost and risk.
Construction capacity is itself one of those dependencies. Large data-center campuses can require
sustained concentrations of electricians, mechanical and HVAC trades, controls specialists, concrete
crews, civil and utility contractors, commissioning personnel and other skilled workers. The same
regional labor pool may also be needed to build the generation, transmission and utility infrastructure
required to serve the project.
Much of that risk is contractually transferred to prime contractors and subcontractors through fixed-
price, schedule, manpower, completion, indemnity and bonding requirements. That allocation does not
create workers who are unavailable. A critical subcontractor that cannot maintain its workforce,
defaults, or withdraws can disrupt multiple dependent trades. Performance bonds and other security
may protect against financial loss, but replacement of a major specialty contractor can itself consume
time, increase cost and threaten the project schedule.

The effect may extend beyond the project. A multiyear data-center build can offer skilled workers
sustained employment, overtime, per diem and compensation that smaller contractors, homebuilders,
public works contractors and ordinary commercial projects cannot match. The resulting competition
can increase regional construction costs and delay unrelated housing, infrastructure and commercial
development.
Illustrative Texas Experience
Texas already provides a practical warning. Reporting from Abilene describes residential builders and
electrical contractors losing experienced electricians to major data-center construction, with resulting
housing delays. Separate 2026 construction-market analysis identifies Texas as one of the concentrated
data-center markets in which skilled-trade constraints are increasing costs and making labor
availability a material project-delivery issue.
The lesson is broader than any single project or trade. A jurisdiction evaluating a major large-load
development should ask not only whether the developer has a construction plan, but whether the
regional contractor and skilled-labor market can support the data center and its supporting
infrastructure on the schedules being represented without creating unexamined cost, completion or
community consequences.
Planned capacity is not delivered capacity. Contractual responsibility is not physical capability. Both
should be tested before schedules and public commitments are accepted.

7. Financial Structure, Debt and Continuity Risk
A project's financial capacity should not be treated as a fact established once at approval. It can change
materially during construction, commissioning and operation. Large data-center developments may be
financed through combinations of parent-company capital, project-level debt, leases, special-purpose
entities, customer commitments, guarantees and other contractual arrangements. The legal entity
holding the permit or property may therefore be only one part of the financial structure supporting
performance.
The central public question is not whether the project uses debt. It is whether the financial structure
remains capable of supporting the obligations on which approval depends.
That inquiry becomes particularly important when a developer, operator, tenant, guarantor or
affiliated enterprise is simultaneously supporting multiple facilities in different stages of development.
A company may have one campus operating, another commissioning, several under construction and
additional projects requiring capital. Financial stress at one level of that structure can affect decisions
about completion, expansion, maintenance, infrastructure payments or continued operation
elsewhere.
Government therefore should understand the principal sources of project capital; material project debt
and lease obligations; the identity and scope of guarantors; whether guarantees are limited by amount,
duration or project; and whether public obligations depend upon continued performance by a tenant,
customer, parent or affiliate that is not itself the permit holder.
The framework should also address foreseeable stress scenarios. What happens if construction costs
materially exceed budget? If commissioning is delayed? If anticipated revenue or customer demand
does not materialize on schedule? If refinancing becomes unavailable or materially more expensive? If
a major tenant, operator or guarantor defaults? If capital must be allocated among several affiliated
projects at the same time?
Those questions matter because public and utility infrastructure may already have been constructed
when financial stress emerges. A financially troubled project should not be able to transfer

unrecovered infrastructure costs, deferred maintenance, environmental obligations, decommissioning
costs or other project-specific liabilities to ratepayers or taxpayers merely because the original
financial assumptions failed.
Financial assurance should therefore be tested not only for its existence at approval, but for its
durability. Guarantees, bonds, letters of credit, reserves and other protections should be evaluated for
amount, duration, renewal, draw conditions, priority, replacement requirements and survival through
restructuring, foreclosure, bankruptcy, ownership change or operator change.
  Financial capacity is not static. Approval should test both the project's ability to perform
  under expected conditions and the protections that remain if those conditions deteriorate.

8. The Minimum Community Protection Framework
Before approval of a major data-center or comparable large-load development, the responsible
governmental bodies should be able to answer at least these questions:
1. Identity and control: Who owns, controls, finances and operates the project?
2. Financial responsibility: What entity possesses sufficient resources to satisfy the project's long-term
obligations?
3. Electricity: What are the expected and maximum anticipated loads, how will electricity be supplied,
what new infrastructure is required, and who pays for it?
4. Stranded-cost protection: What happens if the projected load is delayed, reduced or abandoned?
5. Generation adequacy: What additional generation or firm capacity is required to serve the load
without impairing reliability?
6. Timing and sequencing: For each increment of new load, what generation, transmission, fuel, water
and other supporting infrastructure will be physically operational - not merely planned, permitted,
financed or announced - when that load is energized, and what happens if a required dependency is
late?
7. Water: What are expected and maximum withdrawals, what source will supply them, what
infrastructure is required, and what happens during drought or other supply constraints?
8. Noise: What enforceable limits apply at property lines and affected residences, including low-
frequency and nighttime noise, and how will compliance be measured?
9. Backup generation: How much generating capacity will be installed, what fuel will it use, under what
circumstances may it operate, and how will emissions and noise be controlled?
10. Transportation and construction: Who bears road, traffic and infrastructure impacts during
construction and operation?
11. Construction workforce and subcontractor capacity: Is sufficient qualified labor and specialty-
contractor capacity demonstrably available for site work, utilities, vertical construction, electrical,
mechanical, controls and commissioning, and what contingency exists if a critical contractor cannot
perform or must be replaced?
12. Regional construction-market effects: How may the project's multiyear labor demand affect wages,
contractor availability, housing, public works, commercial construction and the simultaneous
construction of generation, transmission and other infrastructure required to serve the project?
13. Emergency services: What additional fire, hazardous-material, security and emergency- response
capacity is required, and who pays?
14. Expansion: What changes in load, buildings, generating capacity, cooling systems or operations
require renewed governmental review?
15. Transfer: What happens when ownership, control or the operator changes?

16. Monitoring: What information must be reported, how frequently, who reviews it, and how can
government independently verify it?
17. Enforcement: What happens when a material requirement is violated?
18. Financial security: What guarantees, bonds, letters of credit, reserves or other security protect long-
term obligations, and how will their adequacy be maintained?
19. Closure: Who pays for decommissioning, removal and restoration, and is that obligation financially
secured before it becomes necessary?
20. Infrastructure ownership and maintenance: Who will own, operate, maintain, repair and ultimately
replace infrastructure constructed principally or substantially to serve the project?
21. Infrastructure after closure: What happens to project-related infrastructure if the facility closes, and
can it economically and safely serve another development or public purpose?
22. Modernization and retrofit: Which equipment replacements or technological upgrades may occur
under the existing approval, and what material changes in electricity, water, cooling, generation,
emissions, noise or other impacts require renewed review?
23. Project lifecycle: What are the expected economic and physical lives of the equipment, facility and
supporting infrastructure, and what assumptions underlie those estimates?
24. Governmental oversight: Which public body or official is responsible for receiving reports, verifying
continuing compliance, tracking financial assurances and initiating enforcement throughout the
project's life?
25. Cumulative effects: What other large-load developments are existing, approved or reasonably
anticipated in the area, and what are their combined effects on electricity, water, infrastructure, public
services, construction capacity and regional labor markets?
26. Financial resilience and continuity: How is construction and operation financed; what material
debt, lease, guarantee or customer obligations support the project; and what protections remain if the
owner, developer, operator, tenant, guarantor or affiliated enterprise experiences cash-flow stress,
default, refinancing difficulty or competing capital demands across multiple projects?

Conclusion
The United States needs computing infrastructure. Communities also have legitimate interests in
reliable electricity, affordable utility service, adequate water, functioning infrastructure, reasonable
environmental conditions and protection against long-term liabilities created by private development.
Those objectives are not inherently incompatible. Nor does this framework presume that a proposed
data center should be approved or rejected.
The emerging federal debate over ratepayer protection addresses an important part of the problem,
but electricity costs are only one component of a larger set of questions involving water, infrastructure,
ownership, financial responsibility, operations, modernization, community impacts and eventual
closure.
  Large-load development requires lifecycle governance.

Before approval, government should know who is responsible, what that party must do, who pays, who
owns and maintains supporting infrastructure, whether required infrastructure and construction
capacity will actually be available when needed, how compliance will be measured and independently
verified, what financial security stands behind material obligations, whether the financial structure can
withstand foreseeable stress, and what happens when circumstances change.
